title: The Treble Clef radio phoenix and its old nonthermal filaments
comment: 12 pages, 15 figures, 2 tables (excluding Appendix). Submitted to A&A
summary: By inspecting data from the LOFAR Two-meter Sky Survey (LoTSS), we noticed a peculiar bright and filamentary radio source at low-galactic latitude ($b \approx 0.5 °$). This source, detected also in previous radio observations, was originally believed to be a pulsar until Green et al. (2004) suggested that it is located in a heavily obscured galaxy cluster behind the Galactic plane. In this paper, we characterize for the first time the main properties of the host cluster (redshift, mass, temperature, X-ray luminosity, and dynamical status) by using X-ray observations performed with Chandra and SRG/eROSITA. In addition, by combining new uGMRT follow-up data with observations from the e LOFAR LBA Sky Survey (LoLSS), we perform a multifrequency, spatially resolved spectral analysis of the filamentary radio source (VLSS J0318.9+5755, nicknamed here the "Treble Clef" due to its morphology). We conclude that this source is a radio phoenix belonging to a massive, merging galaxy cluster in the Zone of Avoidance. We speculate that its complex morphology is shaped by gas motions generated in the intracluster medium during the ongoing merger, which are also likely responsible for the generation of the candidate radio halo tentatively observed in the cluster center. Owing to its highly filamentary morphology, brightness at $\lesssim$1 GHz, and extremely steep spectrum, reaching values of $α> 4$ between 400 and 650 MHz, this source represents an ideal target for high-resolution, very-low-frequency follow-up observations with LOFAR2.0.

AI.tldr: A peculiar filamentary radio source (the "Treble Clef") in the Zone of Avoidance, originally mistaken for a pulsar, is identified as a radio phoenix in a massive merging galaxy cluster at low Galactic latitude, characterized via Chandra, eROSITA, uGMRT, and LOFAR data.
AI.motivation: To characterize for the first time the host cluster properties (redshift, mass, temperature, X-ray luminosity, dynamical status) of a peculiar bright filamentary radio source (VLSS J0318.9+5755) detected in LoTSS at low Galactic latitude, and to perform a multifrequency spectral analysis to determine its physical nature.
AI.method: X-ray observations with Chandra and SRG/eROSITA to study the host cluster; multifrequency, spatially resolved spectral analysis combining new uGMRT follow-up data with LoLSS observations.
AI.result: The source is a radio phoenix in a massive merging galaxy cluster behind the Galactic plane (Zone of Avoidance); it exhibits highly filamentary morphology, brightness at ≲1 GHz, and an extremely steep spectrum (α > 4 between 400-650 MHz); a candidate radio halo is tentatively detected at the cluster center.
AI.conclusion: The complex morphology of the Treble Clef is shaped by gas motions from an ongoing merger, making it an ideal target for very-low-frequency follow-up with LOFAR2.0.

title: Machine Learning Closure Audits for LSST Photometric Supernova Cosmology
summary: Modern and next generation supernova cosmology analyses rely on end to end simulations to train photometric classifiers, characterise selection effects, validate light curve models, and calibrate distance bias corrections. Standard closure tests based on global Hubble diagram summaries can miss multivariate structure that remains in post correction residuals. We introduce a supervised machine learning closure audit that tests whether measured observables can predict the bias corrected Hubble residuals $Δμ$. We apply the audit to LSST Type Ia supernova simulations from two independent analyses: the M23 mock data sets of Mitra et al. (2023), with spectroscopic redshift and photometric redshift samples, and the predominantly photometric LSST like M25 simulation of Mitra et al. (2025). Standard one dimensional Redshift binned diagnostics explain <1% of the residual variance ($R^2 < 0.01$), suggesting apparent closure. In contrast, out of fold LightGBM models recover up to 98.2% of the variance in the simulated residuals ($R^2 = 0.982$), revealing structured residual predictability. Applying the same audit directly to the real Dark Energy Survey 5 Year (DES 5YR) spectroscopic sample yields a held out $R^2 = 0.725$. SHAP feature attribution rankings are highly consistent between independently trained M25 and DES models (Spearman $ρ= 0.802$), with apparent magnitudes, signal to noise ratios, and redshift dominating the shared predictive hierarchy. The resulting scorecard provides a diagnostic protocol for comparing mock ensembles and real observations, identifying residual non closure before cosmological parameters are unblinded.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a supervised machine learning closure audit to detect multivariate structure in bias-corrected Hubble residuals from supernova cosmology simulations. While standard 1D redshift-binned diagnostics suggest closure (R² < 0.01), LightGBM models recover up to 98.2% of residual variance in LSST-like simulations and 72.5% in DES 5YR real data, revealing hidden non-closure. SHAP feature rankings are consistent across simulations and real data, providing a diagnostic protocol for pre-unblinding validation.
AI.motivation: Standard closure tests based on global Hubble diagram summaries can miss multivariate structure that remains in post-correction residuals, potentially leading to biased cosmological inferences in supernova analyses.
AI.method: The authors apply a supervised machine learning closure audit using out-of-fold LightGBM models to test whether measured observables can predict bias-corrected Hubble residuals Δμ. They apply this to LSST Type Ia supernova simulations (M23 with spectroscopic/photometric redshifts and M25 photometric sample) and real DES 5YR spectroscopic data, with SHAP for feature attribution.
AI.result: Standard 1D redshift-binned diagnostics explain <1% of residual variance (R² < 0.01), while LightGBM recovers up to 98.2% variance in M25 simulations and 72.5% in DES 5YR real data. SHAP rankings show high consistency between M25 and DES models (Spearman ρ = 0.802), with apparent magnitudes, signal-to-noise ratios, and redshift dominating.
AI.conclusion: The supervised ML closure audit reveals previously hidden non-closure in supernova cosmology simulations and real data, providing a diagnostic scorecard for comparing mock ensembles with observations before cosmological parameter unblinding.

title: Effect of post-recombination accretion on primordial binary black hole mergers within virialized dark matter halos
summary: Gravitational waves from binary black hole mergers remain among primary sources for ground-based and space laser interferometers. Primordial binary black holes (PBHs) can form binaries in the early Universe or at the matter-dominated stage in virialized dark matter halos at redshifts $z\sim 7-15$. We study enhancement of primordial binary PBH merger rate in virialized dark matter halos due to baryon accretion in the post-recombination epoch within two accretion models onto individual PBH -- Bondi-Hoyle-Littleton (BHL) and Park-Ricotti (PR), representing two extreme cases of the accretion efficiency. We calculate modification of the initial PBH mass function and their fractional contribution to dark matter. A significant enhancement in the binary PBH merger rate is found for the late three-body channel, which was previously treated as subdominant. In the case of delayed virialization onset at $z<10$, merger rates of dynamically formed PBH binaries are limited by the existing LVK binary BH detections. An increased merger frequency is revealed for PBH binaries with highly asymmetric mass ratios. We also calculate expected detection rates of binary PBH mergers for the TianQin space-based gravitational-wave interferometer and show them to be optimistic in the BHL accretion case even for very low initial PBH abundances $f\sim 10^{-6}$.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how baryon accretion onto primordial black holes (PBHs) in dark matter halos at z~7-15 enhances binary PBH merger rates, finding significant boosts for the late three-body channel and asymmetric mass ratio binaries, with optimistic detection prospects for TianQin even at very low PBH abundances (f~10^-6).
AI.motivation: To understand the enhancement of primordial binary black hole merger rates in virialized dark matter halos due to baryon accretion, and to assess whether such mergers are detectable by current and future gravitational wave observatories.
AI.method: Two accretion models (Bondi-Hoyle-Littleton and Park-Ricotti) are used to model baryon accretion onto individual PBHs in virialized dark matter halos at z~7-15. The initial PBH mass function and dark matter fraction are modified, and the binary PBH merger rate is calculated for different formation channels, including the late three-body channel.
AI.result: Significant enhancement in the binary PBH merger rate for the late three-body channel (previously subdominant); increased merger frequency for highly asymmetric mass ratio binaries; merger rates limited by LVK detections for delayed virialization at z<10; optimistic detection rates for TianQin in the BHL accretion case even at f~10^-6.
AI.conclusion: Baryon accretion can substantially boost PBH binary merger rates, making them more detectable by space-based interferometers like TianQin, even for very low PBH abundances.

title: Joint constraints on gravity and stellar orbital anisotropy in massive galaxies
summary: Strong gravitational lensing combined with stellar dynamics provides a complementary route for testing gravity on kiloparsec scales and probing the internal structure of massive galaxies. However, such studies remain limited by degeneracies among the mass-density profile, stellar orbital anisotropy and external convergence, and by modelling assumptions, especially when only single-aperture velocity dispersions are available. Here we develop a hierarchical Bayesian framework to disentangle gravity and stellar orbital anisotropy from other effects at the population level. By reconstructing the lens mass distribution with a flexible broken power-law model and propagating its posterior uncertainty into the predicted velocity dispersion, we obtain a likelihood for each lens in the plane of stellar orbital anisotropy and an effective mismatch parameter. This parameter encapsulates projection bias, external convergence, cosmological distance ratios and deviations from general relativity via the post-Newtonian parameter $γ_{\rm PPN}$. Applying this framework to 121 galaxy-scale lenses, we find $γ_{\rm PPN}=1.027^{+0.099}_{-0.095}$, consistent with general relativity, and obtain $2σ$ evidence that the stellar orbits of massive galaxies have become more radially biased over the past $\sim6$ Gyr. Forecasts show that future samples of order $10^5$ lenses could enable sub-percent tests of gravity, precise measurements of orbital-structure evolution and complementary constraints on the cosmological matter-density parameter.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian framework is developed to test gravity via strong gravitational lensing and stellar dynamics in 121 galaxy-scale lenses, finding γ_PPN = 1.027⁺⁰·⁰⁹⁹₋₀·₀₉₅ (consistent with GR) and 2σ evidence for radially biased stellar orbits over the past ~6 Gyr, with forecasts suggesting sub-percent gravity tests from future ~10⁵ lens samples.
AI.motivation: To overcome degeneracies among mass-density profile, stellar orbital anisotropy, and external convergence that limit combined strong lensing + stellar dynamics tests of gravity on kiloparsec scales, and to move beyond single-aperture velocity dispersion measurements by modeling population-level effects.
AI.method: A hierarchical Bayesian framework that: (1) reconstructs lens mass distribution using a flexible broken power-law model; (2) propagates posterior uncertainty into predicted velocity dispersion; (3) obtains a likelihood in the plane of stellar orbital anisotropy and an effective mismatch parameter (encapsulating projection bias, external convergence, cosmological distances, and deviations from GR via γ_PPN). Applied to 121 galaxy-scale lenses.
AI.result: γ_PPN = 1.027⁺⁰·⁰⁹⁹₋₀·₀₉₅ (consistent with GR); 2σ evidence for increasingly radially biased stellar orbits in massive galaxies over the past ~6 Gyr; forecasts show future ~10⁵ lens samples could achieve sub-percent gravity tests, precise orbital-structure evolution measurements, and complementary Ω_m constraints.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully disentangles gravity from orbital anisotropy and othernuisance effects at the population level, confirming GR on kiloparsec scales while revealing evolutionary trends in galaxy orbital structure. The method is scalable to future large lens surveys for precision tests of gravity and cosmology.

title: Present Day Cosmic Acceleration from SDSS and DESI BAO: A Call for Finer Tomography of the DESI Bright Galaxy Survey
summary:
The DESI collaboration's Data Release~2 (DR2) provides baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) measurements from over 14 million galaxies and quasars, and a joint analysis of DESI BAO, CMB, and Type~Ia Supernovae reveals a preference for time-evolving dark energy. We quantify this preference relative to SDSS BAO and report three key results. First, DESI+Planck favors a higher $w_0 = -0.41^{+0.21}_{-0.22}$ than SDSS+Planck ($w_0 = -0.71^{+0.19}_{-0.18}$). Second, DESI+Planck prefers a deceleration parameter whose median lies on the decelerating side ($q_0 = 0.10^{+0.21}_{-0.23}$, consistent with $q_0 = 0$ at $1σ$), while SDSS+Planck prefers a negative value ($q_0 =-0.22^{+0.20}_{-0.21}$) indicating accelerated expansion. Third, we argue that this discrepancy arises from the difference in the lowest effective redshift probed by each survey: $z_{\rm eff} \approx 0.295$ for DESI versus $z_{\rm eff} \approx 0.15$ for SDSS.
  As present-day quantities, $w_0$ and $q_0$ are sensitive to the lowest probed redshift: data near $z = 0$ constrain them directly, whereas higher-redshift data rely on extrapolating the dark energy parametrization (here CPL). Reaching $z_{\rm eff} \approx 0.15$, SDSS constrains $w_0$ and $q_0$ in a data-driven way, finding consistency with $w_0 = -1$ and acceleration. Limited to $z_{\rm eff} \gtrsim 0.295$, DESI relies more on extrapolation, driving $q_0$ positive and $w_0$ well above $-1$. Adding the Pantheon+ supernova sample restores low-redshift information, returning $q_0$ to negative values and reducing tension with $Λ\text{CDM}$. We therefore propose that the apparent DESI preference for a non-accelerating present epoch in the BAO+CMB combination reflects redshift sampling rather than new physics, and suggest future DESI analyses adopt finer tomographic binning of the Bright Galaxy Survey sample to access lower mean redshifts and test this conclusion.

AI.tldr: DESI DR2 BAO data combined with CMB shows preference for time-evolving dark energy ($w_0 > -1$, $q_0$ consistent with zero), but this arises from DESI's higher minimum effective redshift ($z_{\rm eff} \approx 0.295$) compared to SDSS ($z_{\rm eff} \approx 0.15$). When low-redshift supernova data is added, DESI results revert to favoring $\Lambda$CDM and cosmic acceleration, suggesting the apparent discrepancy is due to redshift sampling, not new physics.
AI.motivation: To understand whether the DESI preference for time-evolving dark energy and a non-accelerating present epoch reflects new physics or is a systematic artifact of the survey's redshift coverage.
AI.method: Compare DESI+Planck BAO+CMB constraints to SDSS+Planck, and examine how adding Pantheon+ Type Ia supernovae (low-redshift) affects the inferred $w_0$ (CPL dark energy parameter) and $q_0$ (deceleration parameter). Identify the lowest effective redshift probed by each survey as the key controlling variable.
AI.result: DESI+Planck gives $w_0 = -0.41^{+0.21}_{-0.22}$ and $q_0 = 0.10^{+0.21}_{-0.23}$ (median on decelerating side), while SDSS+Planck gives $w_0 = -0.71^{+0.19}_{-0.18}$ and $q_0 = -0.22^{+0.20}_{-0.21}$ (acceleration). Adding Pantheon+ restores negative $q_0$ for DESI and reduces tension with $\Lambda$CDM.
AI.conclusion: The DESI preference for non-accelerating present epoch is due to its limited low-redshift coverage ($z_{\rm eff} \gtrsim 0.295$), forcing extrapolation of the CPL parametrization. The effect is not evidence for new physics. Finer tomographic binning of the Bright Galaxy Survey is recommended to access lower redshifts and test this.

title: When the Environment Speaks: Quantum Signatures in Non-Attractor Inflation
summary: We study the open quantum dynamics of the adiabatic curvature perturbation interacting with a massive entropic scalar environment during an inflationary scenario featuring a transient Ultra-Slow-Roll phase. Working within a Gaussian two-field effective Lagrangian, we employ the exact Transport Equations Method to track the full non-unitary, non-Markovian evolution of the system's covariance matrix across the SR-USR-SR transition. We find that the efficiency of decoherence is sensitive to the background kinematics at horizon crossing. Most importantly, the interaction with the environment leaves distinct observable imprints on the primordial scalar power spectrum: the characteristic interference dip preceding the USR-driven enhancement can be partially or completely erased, the growth slope modified, and oscillatory features induced near the peak. Propagated to second order, these distortions further imprint on the stochastic background of Scalar-Induced Gravitational Waves, breaking single-field predictions and yielding unique spectral signatures potentially accessible to LISA. Our results demonstrate that the quantum environment is not a passive spectator during inflation, but an active agent whose imprint on the primordial universe may be within reach of the next generation of cosmological observations.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how a massive entropic scalar environment affects the open quantum dynamics of adiabatic curvature perturbations during inflation with a transient Ultra-Slow-Roll phase. Using the Transport Equations Method, the authors find that decoherence efficiency depends on horizon-crossing kinematics, and environmental interactions leave distinct imprints on the primordial power spectrum (erasing interference dips, modifying growth slopes, inducing oscillations) and on Scalar-Induced Gravitational Waves, producing signatures potentially detectable by LISA.
AI.motivation: To understand whether the quantum environment during inflation is an active agent that leaves observable imprints on primordial perturbations and gravitational waves, rather than a passive spectator.
AI.method: The authors work within a Gaussian two-field effective Lagrangian and employ the exact Transport Equations Method to track the full non-unitary, non-Markovian evolution of the system's covariance matrix across the Slow-Roll to Ultra-Slow-Roll to Slow-Roll transition.
AI.result: Decoherence efficiency is sensitive to background kinematics at horizon crossing. Environmental interactions can partially or completely erase the characteristic interference dip before the USR-driven enhancement, modify the growth slope, and induce oscillatory features near the peak. These distortions propagate to second order, imprinting on Scalar-Induced Gravitational Waves with unique spectral signatures potentially accessible to LISA.
AI.conclusion: The quantum environment is an active agent during inflation whose observable imprints on the primordial universe may be within reach of next-generation cosmological observations.

title: Gamma-ray bursts reveal the history and faint contributors of cosmic reionization
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures, 1 table, accepted for publication in ApJL
summary: Star-forming galaxies are generally believed to be the main drivers of cosmic reionization. However, the relative contributions of bright and faint galaxies to this process remain unclear. As the most luminous transient phenomena in the universe, long gamma-ray bursts (LGRBs) provide a unique opportunity to probe star formation occurring in both detectable and undetectable galaxies. In this Letter, we present new estimates of the cosmic star formation rate density (SFRD) at $4<z<10$ using Swift LGRBs detected over the past two decades, by considering LGRBs as unbiased tracers of total star formation at high redshifts. Crucially, we find that the new LGRB-inferred SFRD can naturally explain current measurements of hydrogen reionization without invoking extreme ionizing photon production efficiencies or escape fractions from galaxies. Using these LGRB-inferred SFRD values, we further investigate the faintest magnitude limits of high-redshift galaxies, finding a redshift evolution of the limiting magnitudes from $M_{\mathrm{lim}}\sim-14$ to $-15$ at $z\sim6$ to $M_{\mathrm{lim}}\sim-10$ to $-11$ at $z\sim10$. This result provides one independent piece of evidence for the presence of a large population of faint galaxies at redshifts $z\gtrsim6$, as an important complement to our understanding of the ionizing photon budget in the early universe.

AI.tldr: Using Swift LGRBs as unbiased tracers of star formation at high redshifts (4<z<10), the authors derive a cosmic star formation rate density (SFRD) that naturally explains hydrogen reionization without requiring extreme ionizing efficiencies or escape fractions, and predict a redshift evolution of faint galaxy limiting magnitudes (M_lim ~ -14 to -15 at z~6 to M_lim ~ -10 to -11 at z~10), supporting the existence of a large population of faint galaxies at z≳6.
AI.motivation: To clarify the relative contributions of bright versus faint galaxies to cosmic reionization, and to resolve uncertainties in the ionizing photon budget of the early universe.
AI.method: Analyze Swift LGRB data over the past two decades to estimate the cosmic SFRD at 4<z<10, treating LGRBs as unbiased tracers of total (detectable + undetectable) star formation; then use these SFRD values to infer the faint magnitude limits of high-redshift galaxies.
AI.result: The LGRB-inferred SFRD naturally explains hydrogen reionization without invoking extreme ionizing efficiencies or escape fractions; the inferred limiting magnitudes evolve from M_lim ~ -14 to -15 at z~6 to M_lim ~ -10 to -11 at z~10.
AI.conclusion: LGRBs provide independent evidence for a large population of faint galaxies at z≳6, serving as an important complement to understanding the ionizing photon budget in the early universe.

title: The Subversive Role of Excessive External Shear in Concealing Lensing Anomalies
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Comments welcome. Submitted to ApJ. Lens model parameters and performance metrics available in GitHub repository (link in paper)
summary: To best reproduce observed multiply-lensed lensed images, lens models usually incorporate shear attributed to objects unrelated to the lensing galaxy (i.e., external shear): whether it be neighbouring galaxies not explicitly included in the lens model or other cosmic structures along the sightline. When constrained solely by the positions of image counterparts, such lens models, even those utilising simple ellipsoidal mass distributions, can satisfactorily -- if not near perfectly -- reproduce the observed image positions, but often leave significant differences in flux ratios between the predicted and observed images. For the narrow-line regions (NLRs) of quasars, which are too large to be affected by micro-lensing from stars in the lensing galaxy, the flux ratio anomalies thus left are commonly attributed to small-scale structures (sub-structures) in Dark Matter associated with the lensing galaxy. Here, we show that external shear can always resolve, among the quadruply-lensed quasar NLRs studied, position anomalies in lens models constrained solely by the observed image positions, and in addition reduce although not fully resolving flux ratio anomalies when constrained by both the observed image positions and flux ratios -- provided, usually, that the external shear incorporated have strengths that far exceed (as is the common practise) those typically inferred from weak lensing along general sightlines (i.e., cosmic shear). Our work highlights the subversive role of excessive external shear in concealing lensing anomalies, undermining inferences on the characteristics of Dark Matter sub-structures -- and, correspondingly, the nature (mass and temperature) of the Dark Matter particle -- when not sensibly incorporated into lens models.

AI.tldr: Excessive external shear in lens models can artificially resolve position and flux ratio anomalies, obscuring the signatures of dark matter substructures and undermining inferences about dark matter particle properties.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the common practice of incorporating excessive external shear in lens models masks anomalies that would otherwise reveal the presence and characteristics of dark matter substructures.
AI.method: Analyzing quadruply-lensed quasar narrow-line regions (NLRs) with lens models constrained by observed image positions alone or by both positions and flux ratios, comparing outcomes when external shear strengths are set to values far exceeding typical cosmic shear measurements.
AI.result: External shear can fully resolve position anomalies and partially reduce flux ratio anomalies, but only when its strength greatly exceeds what is typically inferred from weak lensing. This overfitting conceals true lensing anomalies that would otherwise point to dark matter substructures.
AI.conclusion: Excessive external shear subverts the identification of dark matter substructures and biases conclusions about the mass and temperature of dark matter particles; shear must be incorporated sensibly and within physically plausible limits.

title: The dynamical origin of the magnetic field distributions in compressible turbulence
comment: A&A submitted, last stages of referee process
summary: Magnetohydrodynamical (MHD) simulations of isothermal compressible turbulence report that the density distribution is well described by a lognormal with a variance proportional to the flow's Mach number. The distribution of magnetic field strength also has a lognormal component, but includes long, power-law-like tails. In this work, we use semi-analytical arguments to predict the distributions of density and magnetic field strength in compressible turbulent flows. Specifically, in the Lagrangian description of the continuity and the induction equations, we model the velocity gradients of the turbulent flow as a simple random process, essentially turning these equations into stochastic differential equations. Integrating them leads to a lognormal distribution for the density field and the strength of the magnetic field. The power-law tails in the magnetic field PDF appear when we introduce intermittent shocks due to sampling rare events. Gradually increasing the frequency of these events, essentially going closer to a continuous process, leads to lognormal-like distributions again. The asymmetry is connected to the relative abundance of slow and fast shocks. An overabundance of fast MHD shocks produces a high-value tail, while the contrary produces low-value tails. We propose that the appearance of power-law tails along lognormals in turbulent flows is the signature of the co-existence of continuous, diffusion-like propagation combined with localized, intermittent events.

AI.tldr: This paper uses semi-analytical stochastic differential equations to model density and magnetic field distributions in MHD turbulence, showing that lognormal distributions arise from continuous diffusion-like processes while power-law tails emerge from intermittent shock events, with tail asymmetry linked to the relative abundance of slow vs. fast MHD shocks.
AI.motivation: To understand the physical origin of lognormal density distributions and power-law tails in magnetic field strength PDFs observed in MHD simulations of compressible turbulence.
AI.method: Semi-analytical modeling using Lagrangian formulation of continuity and induction equations, treating velocity gradients as random processes to form stochastic differential equations, with intermittent shocks introduced as rare events.
AI.result: Lognormal distributions for density and magnetic field strength arise from continuous diffusion-like propagation; power-law tails in magnetic field PDFs emerge from intermittent shocks; tail asymmetry depends on relative abundance of slow vs. fast MHD shocks; as shock frequency increases toward a continuous process, distributions revert to lognormal-like shapes.
AI.conclusion: Power-law tails alongside lognormals in turbulent MHD flows are signatures of coexisting continuous diffusion processes and localized intermittent events, with shock type determining tail asymmetry.

title: Quantifying Environmental Effects on Galaxy Properties using Non-spherical Voids Identified from SDSS DR7
summary: Cosmic voids provide a distinct low-density region for studying the environmental effects of galaxy properties. Using the SDSS DR7 catalog, we identify non-spherical voids via Voronoi tessellation and the watershed algorithm, and classify void galaxies based on their local volume. We compare and find that void galaxies classified by this method are systematically less massive, fainter, bluer, and have higher specific star formation rate (sSFR) than non-void galaxies and all galaxy samples. We then divide void and non-void galaxies into stellar mass bins to focus on the environmental dependence of $g-r$ color and sSFR. By further classifying galaxies into blue/red and star-forming/quiescent populations, we calculate the ratio of blue to red and star-forming to quiescent for void and non-void galaxies separately. Comparing the ratio of the void value to the non-void value for both metrics presents an overall decreasing trend with stellar mass $M_*$ over the $9.4-10.4$ range in $\log[M_*/\mathrm{M}_\odot]$, indicating a stronger environmental effect in lower-mass systems. These results show that our classification of void galaxies in non-spherical voids based on local volume offers a robust approach for quantifying the influence of underdense environments on galaxy evolution.

AI.tldr: Using SDSS DR7 data and a non-spherical void identification method (Voronoi tessellation + watershed algorithm), the study finds that void galaxies are less massive, fainter, bluer, and have higher sSFR than non-void galaxies. The ratio of blue-to-red and star-forming-to-quiescent galaxies between void and non-void decreases with stellar mass, indicating stronger environmental effects in lower-mass systems.
AI.motivation: To investigate the environmental dependence of galaxy properties in low-density cosmic voids using a robust, non-spherical void classification method based on local volume.
AI.method: Voronoi tessellation and watershed algorithm for non-spherical void identification; classification of void/non-void galaxies by local volume; stellar mass binning; division into blue/red and star-forming/quiescent populations; ratio comparison between void and non-void galaxies.
AI.result: Void galaxies are systematically less massive, fainter, bluer, and have higher sSFR. The blue-to-red and star-forming-to-quiescent ratios (void/non-void) decrease with stellar mass over log(M*/M⊙) = 9.4–10.4, indicating stronger environmental effects at lower masses.
AI.conclusion: Classifying void galaxies in non-spherical voids based on local volume provides a robust approach for quantifying how underdense environments influence galaxy evolution.

title: Reconnection diagnostics for vortex tangles in Bose-condensed and superfluid dark matter halos
summary: Bose-Einstein-condensed (BEC) and superfluid dark-matter (SFDM) halos can contain coherent, wave-supported cores whose angular momentum is carried by quantized vortices. When vortices form a tangle, reconnections convert part of the vortex kinetic energy into dark phonons, density waves, Kelvin waves, and vortex loops, providing a microscopic channel by which SFDM vortex structure can affect halo-core evolution. We estimate the dynamical importance of this channel by combining the local Gross-Pitaevskii reconnection law with a halo-scale vortex-line density calibrated against Schrödinger-Poisson simulations. In the minimal model the released energy stays in the dark sector, and standard-model luminosity requires additional portal physics.

AI.tldr: SFDM halos with BEC cores host quantized vortices that can tangle and reconnect, converting kinetic energy into dark phonons, density waves, Kelvin waves, and vortex loops; this provides a possible channel for halo-core evolution. The channel's importance is estimated via combining local Gross-Pitaevskii reconnection law with calibrated vortex-line density, and the released energy remains in the dark sector unless extra portal physics enables standard-model luminosity.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the kinetic energy released by vortex reconnections in BEC/SFDM halos can be a dynamically important channel for halo-core evolution, and whether it can produce observable standard-model signatures.
AI.method: Combines the local Gross-Pitaevskii reconnection law with a halo-scale vortex-line density calibrated against Schrödinger-Poisson simulations to estimate the dynamical importance of vortex-reconnection energy release.
AI.result: In the minimal model, the released energy stays in the dark sector; producing standard-model luminosity requires additional portal physics beyond the minimal model.
AI.conclusion: Vortex reconnection can provide a microscopic channel for energy transfer affecting halo-core evolution in SFDM, but observable electromagnetic signals require new portal interactions.

title: The MAGPI Survey: Evidence for Non-Universal Resolved Dust Attenuation Relations Beyond the Local Universe
summary: We study the spatially resolved relation between dust attenuation ($A_V$) and star formation rate surface density ($Σ_{\mathrm{SFR}}$) in galaxies from the MAGPI survey ($0.25 < z < 0.42$). Using Balmer-decrement-based attenuation maps for 178 galaxies, we investigate whether the locally calibrated resolved $A_V$--$Σ_{\mathrm{SFR}}$ relation remains valid at intermediate redshift by comparing MAGPI with the local relation measured from MaNGA. We find a clear positive correlation between $A_V$ and $Σ_{\mathrm{SFR}}$ in MAGPI, with systematically higher attenuation than in MaNGA at fixed $Σ_{\mathrm{SFR}}$. After matching galaxies in stellar mass ($M_{*}$) and offset from the star-forming main sequence ($Δ$SFMS), MAGPI galaxies remain more attenuated than MaNGA galaxies at fixed $Σ_{\mathrm{SFR}}$. The attenuation excess is strongest for galaxies below the SFMS ($ΔA_V \sim 0.40$ mag), weaker for galaxies on the SFMS ($ΔA_V \sim 0.28$ mag), and minimal for galaxies above the SFMS ($ΔA_V \sim 0.07$ mag). The dependence of the offset on $Δ$SFMS suggests that nebular attenuation on kpc scales is regulated not only by local star formation activity, but also by the global evolutionary state of the host galaxy. Together, these results indicate that the resolved $A_V$--$Σ_{\mathrm{SFR}}$ relation is not universal, and that locally calibrated attenuation relations may not fully describe galaxies at intermediate redshift. This highlights the need for attenuation calibrations that account for galaxy population and redshift when interpreting spatially resolved galaxy properties.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the spatially resolved relation between dust attenuation (A_V) and star formation rate surface density (Σ_SFR) in galaxies at intermediate redshift (z~0.25-0.42) using MAGPI survey data, comparing with local MaNGA results. It finds that MAGPI galaxies show systematically higher attenuation than MaNGA galaxies at fixed Σ_SFR, even after matching stellar mass and star-forming main sequence offset, with the excess strongest below the main sequence and minimal above it. The results indicate the resolved A_V-Σ_SFR relation is not universal and evolves with redshift and galaxy evolutionary state.
AI.motivation: To test whether the locally calibrated resolved dust attenuation-star formation rate surface density relation holds at intermediate redshift, and to understand the physical mechanisms governing nebular attenuation on kpc scales.
AI.method: Analyzed Balmer-decrement-based attenuation maps for 178 MAGPI galaxies (0.25<z<0.42) and compared with MaNGA local relation. Controlled for stellar mass and offset from the star-forming main sequence via sample matching.
AI.result: MAGPI galaxies show systematically higher attenuation than MaNGA at fixed Σ_SFR. Attenuation excess varies with ΔSFMS: ~0.40 mag below SFMS, ~0.28 mag on SFMS, ~0.07 mag above SFMS.
AI.conclusion: The resolved A_V-Σ_SFR relation is not universal; locally calibrated attenuation relations may not fully describe intermediate-redshift galaxies. Attenuation calibrations need to account for galaxy population and redshift.

title: From 2D to 3D: Recovering Turbulent Density Dispersions from Noisy Data
comment: 12 pages, 13 figures, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Turbulence plays a central role in shaping the structure and dynamics of the interstellar medium (ISM), governing the star formation rate (SFR) and the initial mass function (IMF). A key consequence of turbulence is the generation of density fluctuations, which regulate the amount of dense gas available for star formation. Accurate measurements of the three-dimensional (3D) turbulent density dispersion are therefore essential for understanding molecular-cloud structure and star formation. However, observations typically provide only two-dimensional (2D) column densities and are often affected by measurement/detector noise. The Brunt method estimates the 3D density dispersion from 2D column-density maps, but it does not account for finite signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Here, we extend the method to recover the 3D turbulent density dispersion from noise-contaminated observations. Using numerical simulations spanning a range of density perturbation amplitudes and noise types, we identify a characteristic noise wavenumber, k_noise, corresponding to the intersection of the signal and noise spectra. Restricting the Brunt reconstruction to wavenumbers below k_noise yields a denoised density-dispersion estimate that closely reproduces the noise-free result. We provide a practical prescription to determine k_noise directly from the measurement SNR and image resolution. Alternatively, if the noise spectrum is known, it can be subtracted directly from the observed spectrum, eliminating the need to estimate k_noise. The proposed correction recovers the noise-free density dispersion with errors of <~5% for SNR>=3 and <~15% for SNR>=1, enabling substantially more reliable estimates of turbulent density fluctuations from noisy column-density data.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the Brunt method to estimate 3D turbulent density dispersion from 2D column-density maps contaminated by noise, introducing a characteristic noise wavenumber (k_noise) to filter out noise effects, achieving <~5% error for SNR>=3 and <~15% for SNR>=1.
AI.motivation: Accurate measurement of 3D turbulent density dispersion is essential for understanding molecular-cloud structure and star formation, but observations provide only 2D column densities affected by noise, and the existing Brunt method does not account for finite signal-to-noise ratio.
AI.method: Using numerical simulations spanning a range of density perturbation amplitudes and noise types, the authors identify a characteristic noise wavenumber k_noise at the intersection of signal and noise spectra. They restrict the Brunt reconstruction to wavenumbers below k_noise, or alternatively subtract the known noise spectrum directly from the observed spectrum.
AI.result: The proposed correction recovers the noise-free density dispersion with errors of <~5% for SNR>=3 and <~15% for SNR>=1, providing substantially more reliable estimates of turbulent density fluctuations from noisy column-density data.
AI.conclusion: The extended Brunt method enables reliable estimation of 3D turbulent density dispersion from noise-contaminated observations, with a practical prescription to determine k_noise from measurement SNR and image resolution.

title: GalPort: Investigation of the bar in action-angle space
comment: 18 pages, 7 figures, 1 table, Accepted for publication in Astronomy and Computing
summary: GalPort is a Python package for analysing the orbital dynamics of evolving disc galaxy numerical models in action-angle space. The package implements novel numerical methods for efficiently estimating actions, angles, and frequencies across different, particle-specific timescales: on the scale of radial or vertical oscillation and on the resonant libration/circulation timescale. The algorithm allows calculation of these dynamic quantities simultaneously at all time steps of the simulated galactic evolution. With this tool, one can trace orbital behaviour within time-varying galactic potentials and classify orbits (resonantly trapped, circulating, or passing through a resonance) based on their angle evolution. GalPort also includes specialised options for analysing the phase-space structure of a galactic bar in the disc plane and along its major axis. We demonstrate the package's performance on a typical N-body model of a barred galaxy, obtaining the global distributions of actions and frequencies and performing a detailed orbital decomposition. The code is publicly available under the MIT license at: https://github.com/vdzozulia/galport

AI.tldr: GalPort is a Python package for analyzing orbital dynamics of evolving disc galaxy models in action-angle space, using novel numerical methods to estimate actions, angles, and frequencies across different timescales. It classifies orbits based on angle evolution and demonstrates performance on a barred galaxy N-body model.
AI.motivation: To provide a tool for tracing orbital behavior within time-varying galactic potentials and classifying orbits (resonantly trapped, circulating, or passing through a resonance) in action-angle space, which is challenging due to the non-steady nature of evolving disc galaxies.
AI.method: Novel numerical methods for efficiently estimating actions, angles, and frequencies across particle-specific timescales (radial/vertical oscillation and resonant libration/circulation). The algorithm calculates these quantities simultaneously at all time steps of simulated galactic evolution. Includes specialized options for analyzing phase-space structure of galactic bars.
AI.result: Demonstrated on a typical N-body barred galaxy model, yielding global distributions of actions and frequencies and performing detailed orbital decomposition.
AI.conclusion: GalPort enables orbital classification in evolving galactic potentials, with public availability under MIT license for broader community use.

title: Hubble Space Telescope survey of Magellanic Cloud star clusters. Binaries, mass functions, blue stragglers, and structural parameters
comment: 11 pages, 11 figures. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Binary stars are key tracers of the dynamical evolution of star clusters and provide important constraints on stellar populations and mass functions. The Magellanic Clouds host clusters spanning a wide range of ages and masses, offering an ideal laboratory to investigate these properties in regimes poorly sampled in the Milky Way. We aim to characterize the binary populations, mass functions, blue straggler content, and structural parameters of intermediate-age Magellanic Cloud clusters, and to explore their dependence on global cluster properties. We analyze HST photometry for 16 clusters obtained with ACS/WFC and WFC3/UVIS. Structural parameters are derived from stellar density profiles. Binary fractions are measured using the binary map technique, focusing on systems with mass ratios q > 0.7. We derive MFs accounting for unresolved binaries and identify candidate BS populations from color-magnitude diagrams. The fraction of binaries with q > 0.7 ranges from 5% in NGC 2121 up to 13% in NGC 2173, with a mass-ratio distribution that is consistent with being flat on average. By combining our results with literature data, we confirm a clear anti-correlation between the core binary fraction and cluster mass, while no significant dependence on cluster age is found. The clusters follow the established relation between age and core radius, although with substantial scatter at fixed age. Within the narrow age range explored here, clusters exhibiting steeper MFs are found to have smaller core radii. We find no evidence for a correlation between the fractions of binaries and BS fractions. These findings are consistent with a scenario in which dynamical evolution plays a primary role in the formation of binary populations. The connection between MF slope and structural parameters provides new constraints on cluster evolution and suggests a link between MF slope and structural evolution.

AI.tldr: Analysis of HST photometry for 16 intermediate-age Magellanic Cloud clusters reveals binary fractions (with q>0.7) ranging from 5-13%, a flat mass-ratio distribution, an anti-correlation between core binary fraction and cluster mass, and a link between MF slope and structural parameters, supporting dynamical evolution as the primary driver of binary populations.
AI.motivation: Binary stars are tracers of dynamical evolution in star clusters and provide constraints on stellar populations and mass functions. The Magellanic Clouds host clusters with diverse ages and masses, offering a testbed for regimes poorly sampled in the Milky Way.
AI.method: HST photometry from ACS/WFC and WFC3/UVIS for 16 clusters; structural parameters from stellar density profiles; binary fractions via binary map technique for systems with mass ratios q>0.7; MFs derived accounting for unresolved binaries; candidate blue straggler populations identified from CMDs.
AI.result: Binary fractions (q>0.7): 5% (NGC 2121) to 13% (NGC 2173); flat mass-ratio distribution on average; anti-correlation between core binary fraction and cluster mass; no significant age dependence; clusters follow age-core radius relation with scatter; steeper MFs correlate with smaller core radii; no correlation between binary and blue straggler fractions.
AI.conclusion: Findings consistent with dynamical evolution playing a primary role in binary population formation; the MF slope-structural parameter connection provides new constraints linking MF slope and structural evolution in clusters.

title: Euclid Quick Data Release (Q1). Searching for radio-selected \Euclid-dark galaxies in the EDF-N
comment: Paper accepted by A&A, 20 pages, 14 figures, 4 tables
summary: We present and investigate the properties of a sample of radio-selected, Euclid-dark galaxies, identified from LOFAR HBA observations at 144 MHz within the Euclid Deep Field-North (EDF-N). Starting from radio sources lacking optical counterparts in previous surveys, but detected with Spitzer/IRAC, we identified 166 galaxies with no emission at a more than $3σ$ level in Euclid Quick Release 1 (Q1) images, and no matches in the Euclid Q1 catalogue. To minimise contamination from nearby sources, we selected a sub-sample of 88 isolated galaxies. By exploiting multi-band images and catalogues available for the EDF-N, we inferred the physical properties of our sample via SED fitting. The resulting redshift distribution spans $0.4 \leq z_\mathrm{ph} \leq 5.0$. We used recent sub-arcsecond imaging from the International LOFAR Telescope to constrain the nature of the compact radio emission through brightness temperature estimates. By combining this information with the radio excess relative to the infrared/radio correlation (IRRC), we searched for possible active galactic nuclei (AGN) activity. Approximately 40% of our sources show evidence of AGN activity. The Euclid-dark sources detected in the far-infrared are consistent with a population of heavily obscured, massive star-forming galaxies with high star formation rates. Their location above the star-forming main sequence is consistent with similar near-infrared-dark galaxy populations reported in the literature. We also performed a UV-to-radio median stacking analysis, finding that the two subsamples exhibit similar global physical properties and differ primarily in their radio emission. These preliminary results indicate that the wide area covered by Euclid enables the identification of a higher fraction of systems in which intense star formation and AGN activity coexist, likely capturing a key phase of galaxy--black hole co-evolution.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies and analyzes 166 Euclid-dark radio galaxies (88 isolated) in the Euclid Deep Field-North using LOFAR 144 MHz observations, finding ~40% show AGN activity, with the rest being heavily obscured, massive star-forming galaxies above the main sequence, highlighting Euclid's ability to capture a key phase of galaxy-black hole co-evolution.
AI.motivation: To identify and characterize radio-selected galaxies that are undetected in Euclid optical imaging (Euclid-dark) in order to study heavily obscured star-forming galaxies and AGN, exploiting Euclid's wide-area coverage to capture a phase of galaxy-black hole co-evolution that is missed by shallower surveys.
AI.method: Selected 166 Euclid-dark galaxies from LOFAR HBA 144 MHz sources lacking optical counterparts in Euclid Q1 images but detected in Spitzer/IRAC; refined to 88 isolated sources; performed SED fitting using multi-band data, brightness temperature estimates from sub-arcsecond International LOFAR Telescope imaging, and radio excess relative to the infrared/radio correlation; conducted UV-to-radio median stacking analysis.
AI.result: Redshift distribution spans 0.4 ≤ z_ph ≤ 5.0; ~40% show evidence of AGN activity; far-infrared-detected sources are heavily obscured massive star-forming galaxies with high SFRs located above the star-forming main sequence; stacking reveals similar global physical properties between subsamples differing primarily in radio emission.
AI.conclusion: Euclid's wide-area coverage enables identification of a higher fraction of systems where intense star formation and AGN coexist, likely capturing a key phase of galaxy-black hole co-evolution.

title: Beyond traditional emission-line diagnostics: using autoencoders to uncover active galactic nuclei in DESI spectra
summary: The growing volume of spectroscopic data in modern surveys motivates data-driven approaches that complement traditional emission-line diagnostics for active galactic nuclei (AGN) identification. We present a machine learning framework that exploits the full optical spectrum using unsupervised representation learning within a semi-supervised classification scheme. We use the SPENDER autoencoder to compress DESI galaxy spectra into a low-dimensional latent space and classify sources through a k-d tree nearest-neighbor search. The model is trained on 50,222 DESI Main Survey spectra from the Guadalupe dataset and released as part of Data Release 1 (DR1), restricted to z <= 0.5. We validate the performance using labels derived from FastSpecFit's emission line measurements defining seven galaxy classes: AGN, broad-line (BL), composite, star-forming, passive, retired, and Other. The method achieves high accuracies for AGN (0.952) and broad-line AGN (0.965), reliably identifying these sources even in low signal-to-noise spectra and recovering AGN missed by standard single-diagnostic methods. Our classification metrics are benchmarked against traditional diagnostics, and we show they represent lower limits of the model's true performance. We also find that the learned latent space correlates with key galaxy properties such as stellar mass and star-formation rate, demonstrating that it captures physically meaningful information. These results show that unsupervised spectral representation learning, implemented within a semi-supervised classification framework, provides a scalable and effective approach for constructing more complete AGN catalogues for current and future spectroscopic surveys.

AI.tldr: A semi-supervised machine learning framework using SPENDER autoencoder and k-d tree nearest-neighbor search on DESI galaxy spectra achieves high-accuracy AGN classification (AGN: 0.952, broad-line AGN: 0.965), outperforming traditional emission-line diagnostics and capturing physically meaningful latent representations correlated with galaxy properties.
AI.motivation: The growing volume of spectroscopic data in modern surveys necessitates data-driven approaches to complement traditional emission-line diagnostics for more complete and scalable AGN identification.
AI.method: Uses SPENDER autoencoder for unsupervised representation learning to compress DESI optical spectra into a low-dimensional latent space, then applies k-d tree nearest-neighbor search for semi-supervised classification into seven galaxy classes (AGN, broad-line, composite, star-forming, passive, retired, Other).
AI.result: Achieves accuracies of 0.952 for AGN and 0.965 for broad-line AGN; recovers AGN missed by standard single-diagnostic methods, performs reliably on low signal-to-noise spectra, and latent space correlates with stellar mass and star-formation rate.
AI.conclusion: Unsupervised spectral representation learning within a semi-supervised classification framework provides a scalable and effective approach for constructing more complete AGN catalogues for current and future spectroscopic surveys.

title: A machine learning approach to estimating HI deficiency in galaxies
comment: 23 pages, 10 figures. This is the author manuscript prior to peer review; the final published version is available in PASP
summary: Measurements of the HI content of galaxies serve as an important tracer for probing the impact of environment on galaxy evolution. More specifically, the HI deficiency (defined as the difference between expected unaltered and observed HI content of a galaxy) is closely related with environmental effects, which are most significant in large groups and clusters. In this work, we aim to estimate the HI deficiency of ALFALFA galaxies and investigate its relation with galactic environment. Using a random forest machine learning algorithm, we developed a predictive model capable of estimating the original HI content of a galaxy based solely on its optical properties. The model was trained on a subsample of 6 982 isolated ALFALFA galaxies with optical photometric data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). Our predictive model outperforms the traditional approach, in which HI mass is linearly related to optical size (both on a logarithmic scale). The model achieves RMSE $\approx$ 0.22 dex and $R^2 \approx$ 0.80, compared with RMSE $\approx$ 0.26 dex and $R^2 \approx$ 0.70 for the traditional method. We applied this model to predict the expected HI content for non-isolated ALFALFA galaxies, enabling the calculation of HI deficiency. Controlling for the effects of internal factors, like stellar mass and presence of AGN, we find an increase in binned median HI deficiency of 0.15 dex attributable to environmental effects. In addition, we evaluate the temporal evolution of the predicted HI mass, and associated HI deficiency, due to the evolving stellar populations, following a gas removal event.

AI.tldr: This paper uses a random forest model trained on isolated ALFALFA galaxies with SDSS optical data to predict HI content based solely on optical properties, outperforming traditional linear methods. The model enables HI deficiency calculations for non-isolated galaxies, revealing a 0.15 dex environmental impact on HI deficiency after controlling for internal factors, and evaluates temporal evolution of HI following gas removal.
AI.motivation: To estimate HI deficiency of ALFALFA galaxies and investigate its relationship with galactic environment, using an improved predictive model that outperforms traditional linear approaches.
AI.method: A random forest machine learning model was trained on 6,982 isolated ALFALFA galaxies with SDSS optical photometric data to predict original HI content. The model was applied to non-isolated galaxies to compute HI deficiency, controlling for stellar mass and AGN presence.
AI.result: The random forest model achieves RMSE ≈ 0.22 dex and R² ≈ 0.80, outperforming the traditional linear method (RMSE ≈ 0.26 dex, R² ≈ 0.70). Environmental effects cause a 0.15 dex increase in binned median HI deficiency.
AI.conclusion: The random forest approach provides a more accurate estimation of intrinsic HI content, enabling robust quantification of environmental HI stripping. Environmental processes significantly impact HI content beyond internal galaxy properties.

title: Milky Way Atlas: A radial-velocity-resolved, three-dimensional map of H I within 1.25 kpc
comment: 24 pages, 21 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: We present a velocity-resolved three-dimensional map of local atomic hydrogen (HI) within 1.25 kpc of the Sun, tackling the challenge of converting emission from position-position-velocity space into true 3D structure. Our method combines the HI4PI full-sky survey with the Edenhofer et al. (2024) 3D dust map in the framework of Information Field Theory, enabling a joint reconstruction of the local HI density, radial velocity field, and effective line width while also separating emission arising inside the mapped local volume from more distant Galactic HI. The inference is driven by morphological matching between dust and HI structures together with kinematic coherence in 3D space. Synthetic data tests show that the method recovers the local density and velocity structure, even in the presence of substantial contamination from distant emission. The resulting map reveals a smoother, more diffuse local HI distribution than the dust, a declining HI-to-dust ratio toward high dust column densities consistent with the atomic-to-molecular transition, and a velocity field that captures both large-scale Galactic rotation and local non-circular velocities. Independent comparisons with maser and young stellar cluster velocities agree with the recovered kinematics. This HI map provides a new three-dimensional, kinematically resolved view of the nearby atomic interstellar medium and a foundation for localising other velocity-resolved Galactic emission in physical space.

AI.tldr: A velocity-resolved 3D map of local atomic hydrogen within 1.25 kpc of the Sun is constructed by combining HI4PI survey data with a 3D dust map using Information Field Theory, enabling joint reconstruction of HI density, radial velocity, and line width while separating local from distant emission.
AI.motivation: To convert HI emission from position-position-velocity (PPV) space into true 3D structure, overcoming the fundamental challenge of kinematic distance ambiguity and contamination from distant Galactic HI.
AI.method: Combines HI4PI full-sky survey with Edenhofer et al. (2024) 3D dust map within Information Field Theory framework; joint reconstruction of local HI density, radial velocity field, and effective line width; morphological matching between dust and HI structures plus kinematic coherence in 3D space.
AI.result: The recovered HI distribution is smoother and more diffuse than dust; HI-to-dust ratio declines toward high dust column densities (consistent with atomic-to-molecular transition); the velocity field captures both Galactic rotation and local non-circular motions; validated against maser and young stellar cluster velocities.
AI.conclusion: Provides a new 3D, kinematically resolved view of the nearby atomic ISM and establishes a foundation for localising other velocity-resolved Galactic emission in physical space.

title: Chemical diversity of dense cores in Orion B: The role of the environment
comment: 20 pages, 18 figures, accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics (A&A), abstract was shortened in arxiv metadata
summary: Prestellar cores are the sites of the earliest stages of star formation. Dust continuum observations are often used to identify and characterize their properties yet only a small fraction of them was observed and studied in terms of their composition and dynamical status. We explore the chemical diversity of prestellar cores and protostellar cores residing in the Orion B giant molecular cloud selected on their dust continuum emission to provide an unbiased view of their line emission properties and how they vary as function of the core parameters and environment. We make use of the large scale maps of Orion B in 25 molecular lines from which we extract information for a sample of 1001 cores selected using positions extracted from \textit{Herschel} dust continuum observations. The main properties of the core sample are derived using the Principal Component Analysis and additional maps of physical parameters: column density $N_{\rm{H_2}}$, far-ultraviolet (FUV) radiation field $G_0$ and mean volume gas density $n$. Additional high spectral resolution observations of $\rm C^{18}O(1-0)$ serve to evaluate the dynamical status of cores. The average line width of the cores is larger than what is typically expected for prestellar cores of closer star forming regions, which suggests that cores in Orion B are subjected to stronger turbulence affecting their stability. The first factor of the PCA analysis explaining the variation of the detected line intensities is the core column density of molecular gas. The second factor explains how the core chemical composition is strictly linked to their environment, which can be traced by the ratio of the external FUV radiation field over the core volume density, $G_0/n$. The third factor explaining the core chemical diversity is the mean density along the core line of sight, which is also associated with freeze-out and fractionation signatures.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes 1001 prestellar and protostellar cores in Orion B using Herschel dust continuum and 25 molecular line maps, finding that core chemical diversity is primarily driven by column density, environmental FUV radiation relative to volume density (G₀/n), and mean line-of-sight density (linked to freeze-out/fractionation), while cores exhibit stronger turbulence than typical prestellar regions.
AI.motivation: Despite being sites of early star formation, only a small fraction of prestellar cores have been studied in terms of their composition and dynamical status. This work aims to provide an unbiased view of line emission properties and how they vary with core parameters and environment.
AI.method: Extracted molecular line information from 25-line large-scale maps of Orion B for 1001 Herschel-selected cores. Applied Principal Component Analysis (PCA) along with maps of N_H₂, FUV radiation field G₀, and mean volume gas density n. Used C¹⁸O(1-0) high-resolution spectroscopy to evaluate dynamical status.
AI.result: (1) Cores show larger average line widths than typical prestellar cores in closer regions, indicating stronger turbulence affecting stability. (2) PCA first factor: core column density drives line intensity variation. (3) Second PCA factor: chemical composition linked to environment via G₀/n ratio. (4) Third PCA factor: mean line-of-sight density, associated with freeze-out and fractionation.
AI.conclusion: Core chemical diversity in Orion B is governed by three main factors: column density, environmental FUV radiation relative to volume density, and mean density (freeze-out/fractionation). The enhanced turbulence suggests cores are less stable than those in quiescent nearby star-forming regions.

title: Tracing the Evolution of the Balmer Break from Cosmic Dawn to Cosmic Noon with JWST
comment: 22 pages, 16 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to A&A. Comments are welcome
summary: The Balmer break (BB) is a key spectral feature for constraining stellar population ages, star formation histories, and redshifts of high-redshift sources. The redshift evolution and distribution of BB strength, together with the properties of BB galaxies, constrain stellar population characteristics and the nature of star formation across cosmic epochs. However, a systematic and unbiased characterization of BB strengths across the full galaxy population remains limited with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). We aim to characterize the redshift evolution of BB strength over $z=3.5$-10 and its distribution across different epochs using photometry. We also examine correlations between BB strength and key physical parameters within these redshift intervals. We further assess the implications of BB galaxies for the nature of star formation and stellar populations at $z>3.5$. We used the JWST NIRCam photometric observations taken as part of various programs, including CEERS, JADES, FRESCO, and PRIMER. We estimated the BB strength of the objects with two adjacent broadband filters in various redshift windows between redshifts 3 and 10, which exclude strong line contamination. We employ the SED-fitting code CIGALE for both SED fitting and the generation of mock galaxy simulations. We find that the median Balmer break strength (expressed as a flux ratio) increases from cosmic dawn to cosmic noon, from 1.1 to 1.5, primarily driven by the age of the stellar population. These estimations are in agreement with the latest spectroscopic estimations in the literature. We identify objects with extremely large BB strengths (BB$>3.0$) at $z=3.5$-4 and $z=7$-10, indicating strong extinction combined with an old stellar population and the presence of Little Red Dots (LRDs) in the former, and predominantly LRDs in the latter.[abridged]

AI.tldr: This paper uses JWST NIRCam photometry (CEERS, JADES, FRESCO, PRIMER) to characterize Balmer break strength evolution from z=3.5–10, finding median BB strength increases from ~1.1 to ~1.5 driven by stellar age, and identifying extreme BB>3 objects linked to Little Red Dots at both low and high redshift.
AI.motivation: A systematic and unbiased characterization of Balmer break strengths across the full galaxy population at high redshift remains limited with JWST, motivating a photometric approach to constrain stellar population ages, star formation histories, and the nature of star formation across cosmic epochs.
AI.method: JWST NIRCam photometry from CEERS, JADES, FRESCO, and PRIMER programs was used. BB strength was estimated using two adjacent broadband filters in redshift windows between z=3–10, excluding strong line contamination. SED fitting and mock galaxy simulations were performed with CIGALE.
AI.result: Median BB strength (flux ratio) increases from 1.1 at cosmic dawn to 1.5 at cosmic noon, driven by stellar age. Results agree with latest spectroscopic literature. Extreme BB>3 objects are found at z=3.5–4 (strong extinction + old stellar population + LRDs) and z=7–10 (predominantly LRDs).
AI.conclusion: The redshift evolution of Balmer break strength is primarily driven by stellar population aging, with extreme break strengths linked to Little Red Dots, providing constraints on star formation histories and stellar populations at z>3.5.
